title: OpenAI's safety transparency lead David Robinson resigns, calls culture 'broken'
subtitle: After three and a half years and shepherding safety reports for 12 frontier launches, Robinson exits with a public critique of industry pacing.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: David Robinson, who led transparency work for OpenAI's safety team and oversaw safety reports for 12 of the company's frontier model launches, resigned over the weekend of October 3–5. Robinson was a principal architect of OpenAI's Preparedness Framework — the internal process that assesses whether a model's capabilities cross dangerous thresholds in cyber, bio, and self-exfiltration. He spent roughly three and a half years at OpenAI, long enough to count among its longer-tenured employees.

Robinson paired his departure with an essay in The Atlantic arguing that safety practice across frontier labs has fallen behind capability progress. His exit lands days after OpenAI fired three safety researchers — Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni — for allegedly sharing confidential information with an outside AI safety organization. The pattern reads as a disclosure-side rupture rather than a one-off: the people building the public evaluation surface are leaving, and the person leaving loudest ran the public evaluation surface.

The resignation extends a run of senior OpenAI safety departures that started with the Superalignment dissolution in 2024 and continued through chief scientist exits, the Pachocki 'extreme caution' interview, and the firings earlier this month. It also arrives at an awkward moment for the US–China AI safety channel discussions and the White House 'Super Intelligence Accord,' both of which assume frontier labs can self-police. If the people responsible for drafting self-police documents are now publicly skeptical of them, the policy architecture rests on softer ground than it did a week ago.

A takeaway for learners: the Preparedness Framework is a public document, and the resignation note points to it. Read it alongside Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework — the three together map how labs claim to decide when a model is too dangerous to ship. The gap between what those documents promise and what the people who wrote them say in exit interviews is where the real debate lives.
